idiom_name: shared state in an object (usually the companion object), classes keep ordinary instances
implementation_notes: Scala has no static members - classes in Scala cannot have them - so the monostate's shared storage lives in an object (usually the class's companion object): the object is a lazily initialized singleton with the same initialization semantics as Java statics, and class members can reach each other's private members, so class LogSettings { def level = LogSettings.level } over object LogSettings { var level = 1 } reproduces the pattern with no extra machinery. What replaces the classic structure is the object itself: it is the language's documented replacement for statics and it is a first-class value, so the shared state can be implemented as a trait and mixed in, which also gives tests a seam. Prefer immutable vals or passing one instance around; keep mutable object members only for genuinely process-wide state, and guard them with synchronization or an actor.
code_sketch:
object LogSettings:
  var level: Int = 1          // one copy per process, lazily initialized

class LogSettings:
  def getLevel: Int = LogSettings.level      // ordinary instance methods
  def setLevel(v: Int): Unit = LogSettings.level = v

val a = LogSettings()
a.setLevel(3)
println(LogSettings().getLevel)              // 3
pitfalls: Object initialization is lazy: the state is created on first access, and if the initializer throws, the object stays poisoned for the rest of the process (ExceptionInInitializerError, then NoClassDefFoundError on later uses).
A mutable var in an object is a global: every thread sees it and nothing serializes the writes; use synchronized, atomic types, or an actor when the monostate is written concurrently.

Initialization order between objects is not the source order: a companion that reads another object's state during construction can observe it uninitialized (the Scala equivalent of the static initialization order problem).
The object is per JVM/class loader (and per worker in distributed runtimes), never shared across the cluster.
